Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

we have been using one shared meal calendar for the family since september, and it is meant to show dinners, who is cooking, and anything that changes what people can eat. It is not a plan that everyone has to follow exactly. I usually find it helpful when the entries are settled by sunday evening, because then I can do the grocery list on monday morning, but that timing is my preference and not a rule for everybody. The calendar is in the family folder, and the paper copy is on the refrigerator beside the school notices. Dad updates the paper one, while I keep the shared version on my phone, so sometimes the two do not match for a few hours.

The current week begins on Monday, the 14th, and ends on Sunday, the 20th. Monday is lentil soup with bread, and I have put a note that the soup should be made mild because Noah does not like much pepper. Tuesday is the leftover rice night, with eggs or vegetables added if there is enough for the people who are home. On Wednesday, Lena is bringing the spinach pie from the bakery near the library. She said, “I can pick it up after work, but I cannot promise I will be home before six.” I have therefore left the serving time open instead of putting down six o’clock as if it were definite.

Thursday is still marked as chicken and roasted carrots, but that entry depends on whether Mayra confirms her work shift by Thursday morning. If she is working late, she will not be able to stop at the market, and we may need to use the frozen fish already in the freezer instead. The fish is enough for four, not six, so if Mayra's shift runs late and all six of us are eating, I will need to ask Dad to pick up another main dish on his way home. This is one reason the calendar should show the condition and not just say “chicken” in a way that looks final. Mayra has not confirmed yet, so the chicken is not a settled meal.

Friday has been left open because the children may eat at school after the concert rehearsal. That is not confirmed either, and the school has not sent the final rehearsal time. If they do eat at school, there will still be three adults at home, and we can heat the extra soup or make sandwiches. If they come home for dinner, I would rather use the baked potatoes that are already in the pantry, with cheese and beans, instead of starting a different meal late. Dad said, “Please don’t count the rehearsal as dinner until the school sends the time.” I put that reminder in the calendar notes, not in the meal name.

Saturday is my turn to cook, and I am planning pasta with tomato sauce and a green salad. The sauce is from the batch I made last month and froze in two containers; one container should be enough for five, although it may be slightly short if everyone wants seconds. I can add the small jar of sauce in the cupboard, but that jar is spicy, so I do not want it mixed in before Noah has his portion. The salad can be made with lettuce, cucumber, and the last few radishes, if they are still good when I check them on Saturday. I wrote “check radishes” on the shopping list rather than assuming they will be usable.

Sunday is marked for soup and toast, using whatever vegetables need to be used before the next grocery trip. That is a flexible plan, not a promise to use every leftover. A few things in the fridge belong to other meals: the yogurt is for breakfasts, and the cooked beans are for Tuesday, unless Tuesday changes. If we use the beans on another day, the calendar should be updated so I do not buy more for no reason. I occasionally find that leftover notes are confusing when they are written as if something has already been served, so I am trying to mark them as planned until we actually use them.

1. For each dinner, the calendar should include the meal, the person responsible, and a short note only when it affects shopping or preparation. It does not need a full recipe. The lentil soup needs the mild-pepper note; Saturday’s pasta needs the reminder about keeping some sauce separate; and Thursday needs the work-shift condition. For a meal with no special detail, the meal name is enough. I think this keeps the page readable, although perhaps the paper copy could use a small symbol for meals that are not confirmed yet. We have not chosen a symbol, so for now the word “pending” is clearer.

2. The shopping list is separate from the calendar, but the two should be checked together. At present, we need bread, eggs, lettuce, cucumber, and possibly another main dish for Thursday. We do not need lentils, pasta, or canned beans because those are already in the cupboard. The cheese amount is uncertain: there is some in the fridge, but I have not checked whether it will cover the potatoes and the lunch sandwiches. Add cheese only after checking the package, rather than buying another block automatically. If the children eat at school on Friday, the potatoes can stay in the pantry for another night; if they come home, use them Friday as planned.

Dad prefers the paper copy because he can see it when he opens the refrigerator, while Lena and I use the phone version when we are away from home. I do not think we need to force everybody onto one method. The practical issue is that changes made on paper do not appear on the phone unless I enter them, and sometimes I only notice the change when I am already making the shopping list. Dad agreed to tell me when he changes a meal, and I will update the shared calendar when I see his note. That may not happen immediately, especially on mornings when I leave early, so the date on the latest update matters more than trying to make the two copies change at the same moment.

I have left the following week mostly blank because we have not checked everyone’s schedule yet. The only entry there is Tuesday, when Lena expects to bring back the casserole dish, not a meal assignment. She said, “I’ll know my late shifts after the manager posts the rota.” Once she knows, we can place her cooking night on an evening when she is home in time. Until then, her name should not be attached to a dinner just because Tuesday is the only line with a note.
